findings.how_to_check: Run `python -c "import replication.hash_inputs_machineB as h; print('\n'.join(h.input_list()))"` and compare its 15 returned paths against `replication/input_manifest_machineB.md`; check `replication/run_machineA.do` to confirm that `build_linkage_sample1940.do` is never executed; and run `verify_paths.do` to confirm that it still checks the three superseded files.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `build_linkage_sample1940.do` to the Machine-A master execution pipeline (`run_machineA.do` / `Run-MachineA.ps1`), script the transfer to Machine B's expected path, update `verify_paths.do` to remove checks for the three superseded files, and regenerate `replication/input_manifest_machineB.md` on Machine B so it hashes the 15 active inputs and moves the superseded files to the `## Superseded` section.
findings.title: The new denominator artifact is manually transferred and absent from the committed input manifest
findings.what_the_code_does: The builder script `build_linkage_sample1940.do` creates `linkage_sample1940.dta` in Machine A's intermediate folder, but is only invoked via an untracked scratch wrapper (`_run_build_linkage_sample1940.do`) and is not integrated into `run_machineA.do`. Its header notes that the output must be copied manually via Dropbox to Machine B's `$D_FLAGS`. On Machine B, `run_machineB.do` and `hash_inputs_machineB.py` were adjusted to 15 inputs (adding `linkage_sample1940.dta` and dropping three superseded 1940 files), but `input_manifest_machineB.md` was not regenerated and still lists 17 inputs, retains the superseded files, and lacks a hash for `linkage_sample1940.dta`. Additionally, `verify_paths.do` added `linkage_sample1940.dta` but still requires the three superseded files.
findings.why_it_matters: Running `python replication/hash_inputs_machineB.py --check` on Machine B will immediately fail because `linkage_sample1940.dta` is missing from `input_manifest_machineB.md`. Furthermore, an external replicator running the master pipelines from scratch cannot reproduce Tables 5–8 because Machine A's master script does not build `linkage_sample1940.dta`, and Machine B's run will fail if the multi-gigabyte file is not manually copied between machines.

findings.how_to_check: Run `replication/diagnostics/validation_fixed_initials.do`, which proves on the main sample that kept links cannot change validation status under a single fixed 1940 validator and decomposes the share of gains due to re-transcription vs. link selection. In `linkage_analysis.do`, compute the MI match rate using `mi_anc` fixed for both Old and New links to see how much the apparent link quality gain diminishes.
findings.suggested_fix: Report middle-initial validation rates against a single fixed human validator (e.g., `mi_anc` or `mi_fs` across all columns) to isolate true link-quality improvements. If own-transcription validation is retained, label the row explicitly as 'Own-Transcription Initial Agreement (%)' and distinguish it clearly from independent linkage validation.
findings.title: Old vs. New middle-initial match rates switch the validating transcription between columns, conflating link selection with re-transcription
findings.what_the_code_does: For Old links, `miv` is set to Ancestry's initial `mi_anc`, whereas for New links it is set to the ML model's initial `mi_ml`. The code evaluates `count if mi1930 == mi1940` and displays the resulting rates side by side as `MI Match Rate (%)` in Panel A under the heading `Coverage and Link Quality`.
findings.why_it_matters: Middle-initial agreement is used in the historical linkage literature as an external validator of match correctness. By switching the 1940 validating initial from Ancestry to ML between columns, the comparison does not isolate link quality from transcription quality. As demonstrated in `replication/diagnostics/validation_fixed_initials.do:78-79`, for every link kept unchanged between Old and New, validation status cannot change under a fixed 1940 initial (`assert vb_`src'==va_`src' if status==1`). Under the moving validator, however, rates change purely because the ML model re-transcribed 324,768 initials differently from Ancestry. Although the revised captions disclose the own-initial convention, placing this in Panel A under 'Link Quality' attributes transcription shifts to linking improvements. A referee will demand a fixed-validator comparison.

review_limits: No paper draft was supplied; claims-vs-code review was restricted to generated LaTeX table captions, labels, and script comments, so prose claims and text citations could not be checked.

External data directories (on drives F: and Dropbox) could not be accessed, and the Stata pipelines (which require hours and large census files) could not be executed; runtime assertions and record counts were verified by static source code tracing.
The scope was limited to uncommitted working-tree modifications and directly associated linkage/replication scripts, rather than a full end-to-end audit of pre-existing linkage algorithms.

The independence, completeness, and sampling properties of the FamilySearch profile truth set (`mlp_training1930_1940.dta`) could not be empirically validated without access to the underlying graph and crosswalks.
summary: The alignment of linkage denominators and sample definitions across the ABE/JW and HLINK tables with the paper's main table is executed with rigorous numerical assertions and safeguards against Stata missing-value traps. However, the defining denominator dataset (`linkage_sample1940.dta`) remains outside an automated replication workflow, and the committed Machine-B input manifest has not been updated to match the 15 active inputs. In addition, the middle-initial validation rates continue to switch the validating 1940 transcription between Ancestry and ML across columns, confounding link quality with re-transcription quality.
